🌱 For young readers

About ages 8 to 12. Read it together, or on your own.
Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel was a German professor who lived about 200 years ago. He asked a big question: what does it really mean to be free?

Many people say freedom means doing whatever you want. Hegel thought that was only the beginning. Think of a game of soccer. Without rules, there is no game at all, just a crowd kicking a ball. The rules do not take away the players' freedom; they make the game possible. Hegel thought families, schools, jobs and laws can work the same way: good ones help people become who they want to be.

blocks.name: gb-hegel-right
blocks.cap: Hegel's book climbs in five steps, from owning things to living in a free country. Tap each step.

blocks.html:
🧩 Try this

Rules that make things possible. List three games or activities you like. For each, name one rule. Then ask: would the game be more fun, or less, without that rule? Which rules make you more free?

📖 For teens and adults

The full lesson.

G. W. F. Hegel (1770–1831) grew up in Stuttgart, studied theology at Tübingen with the poet Hölderlin and the philosopher Schelling, and taught at Jena, Nuremberg and Heidelberg before he became professor of philosophy at Berlin in 1818. He was nineteen when the French Revolution began, and he spent his life thinking about what it had promised: a world built on freedom. The Philosophy of Right (1820, dated 1821) was his textbook for his Berlin lectures on law, ethics and the state.

By right (German Recht) Hegel means much more than law. He means every way that freedom becomes real in the world: owning things, keeping promises, acting on conscience, family life, work and trade, and citizenship.

blocks.name: gb-hegel-right
blocks.cap: Our summary of the book's three parts, with ethical life divided into its three forms.

blocks.html: The book climbs in three parts. Abstract right is freedom at its thinnest: I am a person, I can own property, I can make contracts. Morality turns inward, to intention and conscience. Ethical life brings the two together in shared institutions: the family, civil society and the state.

Hegel's big claim is that freedom is not only something inside a person. It needs a world to live in: customs, laws and institutions that free people can recognize as their own. He calls this ethical life (Sittlichkeit).

Hegel was one of the first philosophers to give the modern economy its own place in a theory of the state. He had read Adam Smith and the other economists. In civil society each person pursues his own interest, and yet everyone depends on everyone else, like threads in a web. Hegel admired this world of work and trade, and he also saw its dangers: he wrote that great wealth and great poverty grow side by side, and that a society can leave some people with no stake in it. He hoped courts, public authorities and trade associations would hold it together.

At the top stands the state, a constitutional monarchy with a written law, an educated civil service and an assembly of estates. For Hegel the state is not just a contract people sign to protect their property; it is the place where citizens come to see the common good as their own good too.

Hegel's praise of the state is the most argued-over part of the book. Some critics, especially in the 20th century, read it as worship of state power. Many scholars answer that Hegel defended the rule of law, property, conscience and a constitution, and attacked rulers who stand above the law. Both readings start from real passages in the book, so it is worth reading it yourself.
The Preface ends with one of the most famous images in philosophy. Philosophy, Hegel says, does not tell the world what it ought to be; it comes along afterward and understands it.

The same Preface contains another famous line, in Dyde's words: "What is rational is real; And what is real is rational." Some readers took it as approval of whatever exists. Hegel later explained that by "real" he meant what truly lives up to its own nature, not everything that happens to be around.
Thinking Hegel's "right" means only courtroom law. In this book a loving family and an honest day's work are forms of right too.

🔭 Going deeper

Context, the big questions, and how later books answered.

Hegel's students split after his death. "Right" Hegelians stressed his respect for existing institutions and religion; "Left" or "Young" Hegelians, among them Karl Marx, used his ideas to criticize the society of their day. Marx's first major manuscript was a critique of this very book. Later, liberal critics such as Karl Popper (1945) accused Hegel of paving the way for the all-powerful state; scholars such as Shlomo Avineri and Allen Wood replied that this misreads a defender of modern constitutional government. The debate continues.

blocks.text: Hegel and earlier books on this ladder

items: Plato's Republic and Aristotle's Politics: Hegel admired the Greek city, where citizens felt at one with their laws, but thought it left no room for individual conscience.
Locke and Rousseau: Hegel rejected the idea that the state is a contract among individuals, but kept Rousseau's idea of a general will in a new form.
Kant: Hegel's "morality" is his answer to Kant. He praised Kant's idea of duty but thought duty alone is empty without a world of customs and institutions.
Adam Smith: Hegel's civil society takes over Smith's picture of a market linking strangers.
Is freedom doing what you want, or being able to become who you want to be?
Can rules and institutions make people more free? When do they make them less free?
Does a person owe anything to the community that raised them?
Can philosophy only understand the world, or can it change it? (Marx, later on this ladder, gave a famous answer.)

blocks.html: Hegel's other rung here, The Philosophy of History, tells the story of how, in his view, freedom came into the world.

💬 Talk about it together

  1. What rules at home or school make you more free? Do any make you less free?
  2. Hegel thought love, not a contract, holds a family together. What do you think holds your family together?
  3. Is it fair that some people get rich while others stay poor in a market? What could a community do about it?
  4. What does it mean to see the common good as your own good?
  5. The owl of Minerva flies at dusk. Can you think of something you understood only after it was over?

🌱 For young readers

About ages 8 to 12. Read it together, or on your own.
Hegel was a German professor who told the whole history of the world as one big story. In his story, the hero is not a king or a general. The hero is an idea: freedom.

Long ago, Hegel said, people thought only the king was free. Later, in ancient Greece and Rome, some people were free and others were slaves. Over many centuries, people came to believe that every person is meant to be free. That idea took a long time to turn into laws, and it is still being worked out.

blocks.name: gb-hegel-history
blocks.cap: Hegel's four stages, from "one is free" to "all are free." Tap each one.

blocks.html: For parents: Hegel's picture of Asia and Africa was badly mistaken, as later historians have shown. The lesson says so, and it is a good chance to talk about how people judge cultures they do not know well.

🧩 Try this

Your own history book. Draw a timeline of your life so far with five events. Then give it a theme, the way Hegel did: is your story about growing braver, kinder, more independent? Which events fit the theme, and which do not?

📖 For teens and adults

The full lesson.

Hegel (1770–1831) lectured on the philosophy of world history five times at the University of Berlin, from 1822 to 1831. After his death, his student Eduard Gans and later his son Karl put the lectures together from Hegel's own notes and students' notebooks, and published them in 1837. J. Sibree's English translation followed in 1857.

Hegel begins by sorting historians. Original historians, like Herodotus and Thucydides, wrote about events they lived through. Reflective historians look back and arrange the past, sometimes to draw lessons, which Hegel doubts anyone learns. Philosophical history, his own kind, looks for the reason running through it all.

Hegel divides world history into stages, in a famous formula: the Eastern nations knew only that one is free; the Greek and Roman world, that some are free; and the modern Christian world, that all are free, as human beings.

blocks.name: gb-hegel-history
blocks.cap: Hegel's stages, with our notes on how later historians judge them.

blocks.html: Hegel was trying to show that history is not "one thing after another" but has a direction. That idea, that history is going somewhere, shaped a great deal of 19th-century thought, from Marx to many believers in progress.

blocks.text: Passion and the cunning of reason

blocks.html: How does freedom move forward if people act for selfish reasons? Hegel answers that great figures, his world-historical individuals such as Alexander, Caesar and Napoleon, chase their own ambitions, and yet without meaning to they carry history's purpose forward. He calls this the cunning of reason.

Taking Hegel's stages as a fair account of the world's peoples. His picture of China, India and Africa rested on the thin and often prejudiced reports available in Europe in the 1820s, and historians reject it. His lectures are read today for their big idea about freedom, not as a reliable history of those places.

🔭 Going deeper

Context, the big questions, and how later books answered.

blocks.text: Is there a direction to history?

blocks.html: Hegel's lectures raised a question every later philosopher of history had to face. Marx kept Hegel's stages but said the engine is economic, not Spirit. Tolstoy, in War and Peace (later on this ladder), mocked the idea that great men steer history. Nietzsche doubted that history has any goal at all. Many 20th-century historians grew wary of any grand pattern, after seeing what was done in the name of history's supposed direction; others still find the idea of a long, uneven growth of freedom worth arguing about.

items: Does history have a direction, or is that a story we tell afterward?
Do great individuals make history, or does history make them?
Can good come out of selfish actions? Can you think of an example?
How should we judge a thinker whose big idea is inspiring but whose facts were wrong?

blocks.html: Compare Herodotus and Thucydides, Hegel's "original" historians, earlier on this ladder, and Gibbon, a great "reflective" one.

💬 Talk about it together

  1. Hegel said nothing great is done without passion. What are you passionate about?
  2. Do you think people learn from history? Can you think of a time someone did, or did not?
  3. Who is someone in history who changed the world? Did they mean to?
  4. What does it mean for everyone to be free? Is that true in every country today?
  5. Hegel was wrong about many peoples he never studied. How can we avoid judging others without knowing them?

🌱 For young readers

About ages 8 to 12. Read it together, or on your own.
John Stuart Mill was an English thinker who lived in the 1800s. His father taught him Greek when he was three! When he grew up, he wrote a small book with a big idea, called On Liberty.

Mill's idea is simple to say: you should be free to run your own life, as long as you are not harming other people. If what you do affects only you, other people may give you advice, but they should not force you. If what you do hurts someone else, then the community can step in.

Mill also thought people must be free to say what they think, even when most people disagree. Maybe the one person who disagrees is right! And even if they are wrong, arguing with them helps everyone understand the truth better.

blocks.name: gb-mill-harm
blocks.cap: Ten cases, all from Mill's own book. Decide what Mill would say, then see his reason.

blocks.html:
🧩 Try this

Where is the line? Make two columns: "only affects me" and "affects other people." Sort these: what color socks you wear; playing loud music at midnight; eating your vegetables; borrowing a friend's bike without asking; reading a book everyone else thinks is boring. Were any hard to sort? Why?

📖 For teens and adults

The full lesson.

John Stuart Mill (1806–1873) was raised by his father, the philosopher James Mill, in a famous experiment in education: Greek at three, Latin at eight, economics and logic before he was fourteen. At twenty he fell into a deep depression and found his way out partly through poetry, especially Wordsworth. He worked for the East India Company for thirty-five years, served one term in Parliament, and wrote on logic, economics, ethics and politics.
He planned On Liberty with Harriet Taylor, his close friend for twenty years and then his wife. She died in 1858; the book came out in 1859, dedicated to her memory.

Mill applies this only to adults "in the maturity of their faculties," not to children. And he worries about two kinds of control: laws, and the quieter pressure of public opinion and custom, which he calls a social tyranny that can be worse than many kinds of political oppression.

blocks.name: gb-mill-harm
blocks.cap: Mill's own cases, from the drunken policeman to the unsafe bridge.

blocks.html: Chapter II gives three reasons:

items: The silenced opinion may be true. To silence it is to claim we cannot be wrong.
It may hold part of the truth, and the accepted view is rarely the whole of it.
Even a true belief, if never challenged, becomes a dead dogma, held without understanding.

blocks.html: Mill draws a line at incitement: the opinion that grain dealers starve the poor may be printed in a newspaper, but may be punished when it is shouted to an excited mob outside a grain dealer's house.

Chapter III praises individuality. Human nature, Mill writes, is not a machine built to a pattern but a tree that needs to grow on all sides. Society gains from "experiments of living," because no one knows in advance which ways of life will turn out best.

Critics, then and now, ask where "harm to others" begins. Almost anything a person does affects someone. Mill's early critic James Fitzjames Stephen (1873) argued that society has always rightly enforced some morals. Others say Mill underrates how much people need shared customs. Defenders answer that the principle is meant to put the burden of proof on anyone who wants to restrict liberty. The book is still at the center of these debates.

Reading Mill as saying "anything goes." He wanted people to advise, persuade and even avoid one another freely; what he opposed was force, by law or by social punishment, over acts that concern only oneself.

🔭 Going deeper

Context, the big questions, and how later books answered.

items: Milton's Areopagitica (1644) had argued for a free press: let truth and falsehood grapple.
Tocqueville's Democracy in America gave Mill the fear of a "tyranny of the majority"; Mill reviewed both volumes.
Mill's Utilitarianism, his next rung, rests liberty on the long-run happiness of humanity, not on natural rights, an argument critics have questioned ever since.
Humboldt, a German thinker, gave Mill the motto on his title page: the full development of each person in its richest diversity.
Is offending someone a kind of harm?
Should people be stopped from harming themselves? Always, never, or sometimes?
Can public opinion be a tyrant even when the law is fair?
What do you learn by hearing the best case for a view you reject?

blocks.html:
💬 Talk about it together

  1. Can you think of something that only affects you? Is anything truly only about you?
  2. Have you ever changed your mind after hearing someone disagree with you?
  3. Mill thought being different helps everyone learn. Do you agree?
  4. When should a parent step in to stop a child from a risk? When should they let the child decide?
  5. Why might people be afraid to say what they think, even where the law allows it?

🌱 For young readers

About ages 8 to 12. Read it together, or on your own.

How do you decide what is the right thing to do? John Stuart Mill gave one famous answer: do what brings the most happiness to everyone it touches, and count everyone's happiness the same, including your own.

Mill added something important. Some kinds of happiness are higher than others. The joy of reading a great story, learning something hard, or helping a friend is worth more, he said, than the quick fun of a candy bar, even if the candy feels good too.

blocks.name: gb-mill-happy
blocks.cap: Move the sliders: how many people does each choice affect, and how much? Try the late-music example.

blocks.html:
🧩 Try this

Happiness count. Your family is choosing a Saturday activity. List three ideas. For each, guess how happy it would make each person, from 0 to 5, and add up the totals. Does the biggest total feel like the fairest choice? What if one person would be miserable?

📖 For teens and adults

The full lesson.

Mill (1806–1873) was raised on the ideas of Jeremy Bentham, a friend of his father, who taught that right and wrong should be measured by pleasure and pain. Mill spent his life defending and reshaping that idea. Utilitarianism first appeared as three articles in Fraser's Magazine in 1861 and as a book in 1863. Considerations on Representative Government came out in 1861. Both are in the Britannica set with On Liberty.

Two things make this an ethics, not selfishness. The happiness that counts is that of everyone affected; and each person counts equally. Mill quotes Bentham's rule: everybody to count for one, nobody for more than one.

blocks.name: gb-mill-happy
blocks.cap: A simple sum: people times happiness each. Try the late-music example to see the classic objection.

blocks.title: A simple sum
blocks.q: Choice A makes 12 people each 2 units happier. Choice B spares 1 person a loss of 9 units. Which has the greater total?
steps: A simple sum prefers A, 24 to 9.
blocks.a: A, by a simple sum. Many readers feel uneasy at this, which is why Mill's chapter on justice matters.

blocks.html: Critics said a life aimed at pleasure was "a doctrine worthy only of swine." Mill answered that pleasures differ in quality, not only amount. Who can judge? Those who have known both kinds.

The strongest objection is that a large total could seem to justify a serious wrong to a few. Mill's last chapter answers that the rules of justice, which protect each person's security and rights, guard the most vital part of everyone's well-being, so a society that breaks them for a short-term gain loses far more in the long run. Critics such as W. D. Ross and, later, John Rawls replied that this still makes rights depend on a sum, and that some things are wrong whatever the sum. Defenders have answered with refined versions of the theory. It remains one of the main schools of ethics.

In Considerations on Representative Government Mill argues that the best government is one in which the whole people share in ruling, through representatives they elect, because it protects everyone's interests and because taking part in public life makes citizens wiser and more active. He feared that a majority could ignore minorities, so he backed proportional representation, following Thomas Hare's plan. He argued for votes for women, and in Parliament in 1867 he proposed changing "man" to "person" in the Reform Bill; it was defeated. He also proposed extra votes for the more educated, an idea most readers then and since have rejected.
Thinking utilitarianism means "do what makes you happy." Mill insists that the agent must be as impartial as "a disinterested and benevolent spectator."

🔭 Going deeper

Context, the big questions, and how later books answered.

blocks.text: Mill and the conversation about ethics

items: Aristotle's Ethics also puts happiness at the center, but means a life of virtue and excellence, not a sum of pleasures. Mill's higher pleasures move toward Aristotle.
Kant argued that the morality of an act lies in its motive and its rule, not its results. Mill thought Kant's test, when applied, quietly appeals to consequences.
Hume and Smith, earlier on this ladder, grounded morals in feeling and sympathy; Mill's "social feelings" build on them.
Nietzsche, later on this ladder, mocked the English moralists who made happiness the goal.
Can happiness be measured or added up?
Is it ever right to make one person suffer so that many can be happy?
Are some pleasures really better than others? Who gets to say?
Why might taking part in government make people better citizens?

blocks.html:
💬 Talk about it together

  1. What is the difference between something that makes you happy for a minute and something that makes you happy for a long time?
  2. Is the choice that makes the most people happy always the fair one?
  3. Would you rather be "Socrates dissatisfied" or "a fool satisfied"? Why?
  4. When your family decides something together, does everyone count the same?
  5. Why do you think Mill wanted women to be able to vote, long before they could?

🌱 For young readers

About ages 8 to 12. Read it together, or on your own.
Søren Kierkegaard (say KEER-kuh-gard) lived in Copenhagen, Denmark, in the 1800s. He loved to walk the city streets talking with everyone he met, and he wrote many books, some under made-up names.

One of them, Fear and Trembling, is about a very old story from the Bible: Abraham, who trusted God even when he was asked to do something terribly hard, and how in the end his son Isaac was safe. Kierkegaard asked: what does it mean to trust that much? He thought real faith is not easy or ordinary, but the hardest and bravest thing a person can do.

For parents: the Abraham and Isaac story (Genesis 22) can upset young children. You may prefer to talk about the book's other big idea: doing what you believe is right even when no one else understands you.

blocks.name: gb-kierkegaard-stages
blocks.cap: Kierkegaard pictured life as steps, each asking more of a person. Tap each step.

blocks.html:
🧩 Try this

A brave choice. Think of a time someone did something hard because they believed it was right, even though others did not understand: in a story, in history or in your family. What made it brave? Draw or write about it.

📖 For teens and adults

The full lesson.

Søren Kierkegaard (1813–1855) was the son of a wealthy, deeply religious Copenhagen merchant. In 1841 he broke off his engagement to Regine Olsen, whom he loved, a choice that haunted him and many of his books. Between 1843 and 1846 he poured out a stream of works under pen names, each written from a different point of view. Fear and Trembling appeared on October 16, 1843, signed Johannes de silentio ("John of silence").

No excerpts here. The book was first translated into English in 1939 (Robert Payne) and 1941 (Walter Lowrie), so no English version is yet in the public domain in the U.S. This lesson describes it in our own words; libraries carry several good translations.

The book opens by retelling the story of Abraham, who is told to give up his son Isaac on Mount Moriah and who, at the last moment, receives him back. The narrator imagines the three-day journey four different ways, then confesses that he cannot understand Abraham. He can admire him, he says, but he cannot think his way into his faith.

Kierkegaard's target is his own age. Educated people in Denmark, influenced by Hegel, liked to say they had "gone further" than faith, into philosophy. The book replies that they had never reached faith in the first place, and that it is far harder than they thought.

blocks.name: gb-kierkegaard-stages
blocks.cap: Our summaries of the stages and of the book's three figures.

items: The tragic hero, like King Agamemnon in the Greek story, gives up what he loves for a higher duty that everyone can understand. He stays within ethics, and his people weep with him.
The knight of infinite resignation gives up what he loves and makes peace with the loss, inwardly free.
The knight of faith gives everything up and, at the same time, trusts he will receive it back. The narrator says such a person might look like an ordinary, cheerful shopkeeper.

blocks.html: The core of the book asks three questions. Is there a teleological suspension of the ethical, a higher purpose (Greek telos, end) that can set ordinary duty aside? Is there an absolute duty to God? And was Abraham right to keep silent, since he could not explain himself to anyone? In each case the narrator says: if not, then Abraham is lost, and if so, then faith is a paradox that reason cannot master.

Kierkegaard presents this as a portrait of Christian faith as he understood it: a personal relationship to God, chosen in "fear and trembling" (the phrase comes from St. Paul's letter to the Philippians), not a set of comfortable ideas. He wanted readers to face the question for themselves, which is why he hid behind a narrator rather than lecturing.

Some readers, religious and secular, have worried that placing faith above ethics could seem to excuse wrongdoing in God's name; the philosopher Martin Buber pressed this worry in the 20th century. Defenders point out that the narrator says no one can use Abraham as an excuse, since the knight of faith is utterly alone and cannot appeal to anyone. Others read the book less as a rule for action than as a study of what trust, sacrifice and love demand.

Assuming the narrator speaks for Kierkegaard in every line. Kierkegaard used pen names on purpose, so readers would meet a point of view, not an authority. In his own name he later wrote that the pen-name books were not his direct teaching.

🔭 Going deeper

Context, the big questions, and how later books answered.

items: Hegel, earlier in this era, built a system in which faith is taken up into philosophy. Kierkegaard's whole authorship protests that a living person cannot be fitted into a system.
Augustine's Confessions and Pascal's Pensées, earlier on this ladder, also speak of faith as the heart's commitment, beyond what reason can prove.
Dostoevsky, later in this era, writes in the Grand Inquisitor about freedom and faith; readers often pair the two.
In the 20th century, existentialist writers, religious and not, claimed Kierkegaard as a founder.
Is there anything a person might owe that is higher than ordinary duty?
Can you admire someone you cannot understand?
Is it ever right to keep your reasons to yourself?
Why might a writer speak through an invented narrator?

blocks.html:
💬 Talk about it together

  1. What is something that is hard to trust? What helps you trust?
  2. Kierkegaard said the bravest person might look like an ordinary shopkeeper. Do you know someone quietly brave?
  3. Have you ever done something right that others did not understand?
  4. Why might someone hide their name when writing a book?
  5. What is the difference between giving something up and being at peace about it?

🌱 For young readers

About ages 8 to 12. Read it together, or on your own.
Friedrich Nietzsche (say NEE-chuh) was a German thinker with a huge mustache and an even bigger habit of asking hard questions. He became a university professor at only 24.

Nietzsche's favorite question was: where did our ideas come from? He thought people often believe things just because everyone around them does, and that even great thinkers see the world from their own point of view without noticing it.

blocks.name: gb-perspective
blocks.cap: Move the slider. Is it a circle or a rectangle? It depends on where you stand.

blocks.html: Try the picture above: the same can looks like a circle from on top and a rectangle from the side. Nietzsche thought ideas can be like that. It helps to walk around them and look from many sides.

For parents: this is a book for older teens and adults. Nietzsche writes harshly about religion, democracy and women, and some sentences are meant to shock. The lesson explains his main ideas and the main criticisms.

🧩 Try this

Walk around an idea. Pick a family rule, such as "no screens at dinner." Write what it looks like from three points of view: a parent, a kid, and a grandparent. Did the rule look different from each side?

📖 For teens and adults

The full lesson.

Friedrich Nietzsche (1844–1900), a Lutheran pastor's son, was made professor of classical philology at Basel at 24. Ill health forced him to retire at 34, and for ten years he wandered between boarding houses in Switzerland and Italy, writing book after book. Beyond Good and Evil: Prelude to a Philosophy of the Future (1886), printed at his own expense, gathers his ideas in 296 numbered sections, many of them short aphorisms, and ends with a poem. In 1889 he collapsed into a mental illness from which he never recovered.
Nietzsche begins by turning philosophy on itself. Philosophers claim to follow pure reason, he says, but they start from what they already want to believe and then find reasons.

He questions even Descartes's "I think": how do we know there is an "I" that does the thinking? And he asks whether truth is always what we need. What matters, he says provocatively, is whether a belief furthers life. Behind all of this stands his idea of perspective: there is no view from nowhere.

blocks.name: gb-perspective
blocks.cap: One object, many true views; none is the whole.

blocks.html: The middle chapters ask where moral codes came from, as a naturalist might ask where a species came from. In "What is Noble?" Nietzsche sketches two types. Master morality starts from the self-respect of the strong, who call themselves "good" and the rest "bad." Slave morality starts from the resentment of the weak, who call the strong "evil" and praise humility, pity and patience. He argues that Christianity and modern democracy grew from the second. He developed this a year later in On the Genealogy of Morals.

Nietzsche does not simply say "anything goes." He wants a revaluation of values: philosophers of the future who will question inherited values truthfully and create new ones. He admired self-discipline, honesty with oneself, and the courage to stand alone.

Critics answer Nietzsche on several fronts. If every view is only a perspective, so is his own, which seems to undercut it. Many find his praise of the strong careless of the weak, and his remarks on women plainly prejudiced. Religious thinkers reply that he mistakes Christian love for weakness. After his death his sister, Elisabeth Förster-Nietzsche, edited his papers to suit her nationalist and anti-Semitic views, and the Nazis later claimed him. Nietzsche himself despised the anti-Semites of his day and broke with his publisher over them; scholars since Walter Kaufmann (1950) have shown how badly his work was bent.

Reading one shocking aphorism as Nietzsche's whole view. He wrote to provoke, often tried out positions and argued against himself, and in another book asked his readers to read him slowly and carefully.

🔭 Going deeper

Context, the big questions, and how later books answered.

items: Plato: the Preface calls Plato's "pure spirit and the good in itself" the worst of errors; Nietzsche's whole book is an argument with the idea of a truer world behind this one.
Descartes and Kant: Chapter I questions the certainty of the "I think" and Kant's claims about what the mind supplies.
Darwin: Nietzsche borrowed the idea of a natural history of morals but rejected the Darwinians' focus on mere survival.
Mill and the utilitarians: Nietzsche mocked the aim of comfort and happiness for the greatest number.
Dostoevsky, later in this era, whom Nietzsche read and admired, asked from the other side what happens to morals when faith is lost.
Can we ever step outside our own point of view?
Where do our ideas of good and bad come from? Does knowing their history change whether they are true?
Is humility a strength or a weakness?
What does Nietzsche's warning about monsters and abysses mean in everyday life?

blocks.html:
💬 Talk about it together

  1. Can you think of something that looks different depending on where you stand?
  2. Why do people often believe what everyone around them believes?
  3. Nietzsche admired people who think for themselves. How can you tell if you are doing that?
  4. "He who fights with monsters should be careful lest he become a monster." Can you think of a story where that happens?
  5. Is it fair to judge a writer by how others misused his books?

About ages 8 to 12. Read it together, or on your own.

In 1831 a young Frenchman named Alexis de Tocqueville (say TOKE-vil) sailed to the United States with his best friend, Gustave de Beaumont. They were supposed to study prisons. But Tocqueville wanted to understand something much bigger: how a whole country could govern itself without a king.

For nine months they traveled by stagecoach, horseback and steamboat, from New England to the frontier forests, down the Mississippi to New Orleans, and back to Washington. They talked to farmers, lawyers, pioneers and the president. Then Tocqueville went home and wrote a famous book about what he saw.

blocks.name: gb-tocqueville-journey
blocks.cap: Follow Tocqueville's journey stop by stop. Tap Next.

blocks.html: What surprised him most? Americans were more equal than the people of Europe, and they loved to join together to get things done: to build a school, start a library or help neighbors, without waiting for the government to do it.

🧩 Try this

Be Tocqueville. Imagine a visitor from another country spending a week in your town. Write a short letter home as that visitor: what three things would surprise them most? What would they admire, and what might worry them?

📖 For teens and adults

The full lesson.

Alexis de Tocqueville (1805–1859) came from an old French noble family; several relatives had died in the Terror of the French Revolution. A young magistrate, he sailed with Gustave de Beaumont in 1831 on an official mission to study American prisons. They landed at Newport in May 1831 and left New York in February 1832. Volume 1 of Democracy in America came out in 1835, Volume 2 in 1840, both translated into English by Henry Reeve. Tocqueville later served in the French parliament and, briefly in 1849, as foreign minister.

blocks.name: gb-tocqueville-journey
blocks.cap: Our sketch map of the journey, with a note for each stop.

blocks.html: Tocqueville thought equality was the great fact of the modern world, coming to Europe too, whether Europeans liked it or not. He wrote to help his countrymen see both its blessings and its dangers, so they could keep liberty alive within it.

items: Local self-government. In the New England township, citizens run their own affairs. Tocqueville thought this is where Americans learn to be free.
Federalism and the Constitution, which he studied closely, along with The Federalist.
Courts and juries, which teach ordinary people the habits of law.
A free press, many newspapers rather than a few.
Religion, separate from the state, which he thought shaped American habits of self-restraint.
Associations, his most famous observation:

blocks.html: Tocqueville admired America, but he was not a cheerleader. He warned of the tyranny of the majority, not mainly through unjust laws but through the pressure of opinion: "I know no country in which there is so little true independence of mind and freedom of discussion as in America," he wrote, in Reeve's words. He worried that individualism would lead people to retreat into private life and leave public affairs to others, and that a gentle, all-providing government, a soft despotism, could keep citizens in a kind of permanent childhood.

He wrote at length about the three races of America. He judged slavery a great evil that degraded the society that practiced it, foresaw grave conflict over it, and described the forced removal of Native American nations with sorrow, having watched Choctaw families cross the icy Mississippi at Memphis.
Tocqueville's method was to look beneath laws at habits of the heart: the customs, beliefs and daily practices that make a free government work or fail.
Reading Tocqueville as simply praising or simply criticizing America. He set out the strengths and the dangers side by side, and readers of every political leaning have found support in him.

🔭 Going deeper

Context, the big questions, and how later books answered.

items: Montesquieu, whom Tocqueville read constantly, taught him to study how laws fit a people's customs and circumstances.
The Federalist (earlier on this ladder; see the American History & Civics Ladder's Federalist Papers) gave him the American founders' own account of their Constitution.
Mill, next to him in this era, reviewed both volumes and took from them the fear of the tyranny of the majority.
Tocqueville's later book, The Old Regime and the Revolution (1856), asked why France's revolution ended in centralized power.
Can equality and liberty grow together, or do they pull against each other?
Why might people in a free country stop speaking their minds?
What do clubs, teams and volunteer groups do for a community?
Is it easier for an outsider to see a country clearly?

blocks.html:
💬 Talk about it together

  1. What groups or clubs does your family belong to? What do they do that the government does not?
  2. Tocqueville worried people might go along with the crowd. Have you ever been afraid to disagree with a group?
  3. What would a visitor from far away notice first about your town?
  4. Why do you think Tocqueville thought local government was a school of freedom?
  5. Tocqueville saw both good and bad in America. Why is it important to see both in something you love?

🌱 For young readers

About ages 8 to 12. Read it together, or on your own.
In 1848 two young Germans, Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels, wrote a short booklet called The Communist Manifesto. A manifesto is a public statement of what a group believes and wants.

They lived at a time when many people worked long hours in new factories for very low pay, and children worked too. Marx and Engels believed history is a long struggle between rich and poor groups, and they predicted that the workers would one day take over the factories and share everything.

Their ideas became some of the most argued-about in history. Many predictions did not come true, and the countries that later tried to build their ideas set up governments that took away people's freedom and caused great suffering. People still read the booklet to understand those events and the world of factories it describes.

blocks.name: gb-manifesto
blocks.cap: Switch between the Manifesto's own story and what critics and history said.

blocks.html:
🧩 Try this

Then and now. Look up or ask about what work was like for children in factories in the 1840s. Make two lists: "work in 1848" and "work today." What changed? Who changed it? (Many reformers of different views worked on child labor laws.)

📖 For teens and adults

The full lesson.

Karl Marx (1818–1883) studied philosophy in Berlin among the "Young Hegelians" and became a radical journalist. Friedrich Engels (1820–1895), son of a textile manufacturer, worked in his family's cotton business in Manchester and wrote The Condition of the Working Class in England (1845). The two met in Paris in 1844 and became lifelong partners in writing. A small group, the Communist League, asked them for a statement of its program; Marx wrote most of the final text, and it was printed in London in February 1848, in German. Revolutions broke out across Europe that same spring, though the pamphlet had little to do with them. Samuel Moore's English translation, edited by Engels, appeared in 1888.

Section I tells the rise of the bourgeoisie, the modern class of owners. Surprisingly, it praises them: they swept away feudal privileges, built world markets and created more productive power in a century than all earlier ages. But, the authors argue, this system also creates the proletariat, workers who own nothing but their labor, and the two classes must clash. They predicted that workers would grow poorer and more united until they overthrew the owners.

Section II answers objections and lists ten measures for a workers' government, including the abolition of private property in land, a heavily graduated income tax, the end of inheritance, state ownership of banks and transport, and free education in public schools along with the end of children's factory labor. Section III criticizes other socialists; Section IV calls for revolution.

blocks.name: gb-manifesto
blocks.cap: The Manifesto's story, then the record. Our summaries.

blocks.html: Few short texts have had greater effect. The Manifesto became a founding document for socialist and communist movements worldwide. Its attention to economic life and social class influenced how historians and social scientists study the past, including many who reject its conclusions.

items: Failed predictions. In industrial countries, wages and living standards rose greatly after 1848 instead of sinking; middle classes grew rather than vanishing; revolutions came first in largely rural Russia and China, not in industrial Britain.

Economics. Economists of most schools argue that markets, prices and private property are needed to coordinate production; the Austrian economists Ludwig von Mises and Friedrich Hayek argued that central planning cannot do it.
Power. Critics warned, from the 19th century on, that abolishing private property would place all economic power in the hands of the state.

The 20th-century record. States that claimed Marx's ideas, beginning with the Soviet Union, set up one-party rule and state-run economies. Their record includes famines, labor camps, mass executions and the suppression of basic freedoms, costing many millions of lives. The Soviet Union broke up in 1991. Some Marxists argue these states betrayed Marx's aims; most historians and critics reply that the outcomes followed from concentrating all power and property in a single party.

blocks.html: Treating the Manifesto as a description of any country's actual history. It is a call to action with predictions, written in a few weeks for a small group in 1848. Read it as an argument, and weigh it against what happened.

🔭 Going deeper

Context, the big questions, and how later books answered.

blocks.text: The Manifesto in the great conversation

items: Hegel gave Marx the idea that history moves in stages toward a goal; Marx replaced Spirit with economic forces.
Adam Smith and the classical economists described the market that Marx set out to criticize, in Capital, the next rung.
Rousseau's Discourse on Inequality had already blamed private property for many social ills.
Mill and Tocqueville, in this same era, worried about poverty and the working class too, but defended liberty, property and gradual reform.
Is history mainly driven by economics, by ideas, by individuals or by chance?
When a book's predictions fail, what, if anything, is still worth learning from it?
Why might a plan to make everyone equal end in great inequality of power?
What reforms improved the lives of factory workers in the 1800s, and who made them happen?

blocks.html:
💬 Talk about it together

  1. What was life like for children who worked in factories in the 1840s? What changed it?
  2. Marx and Engels said history is a struggle between groups. Can you think of other ways to tell history?
  3. Why do you think so many of the book's predictions did not come true?
  4. Why is it dangerous for one group to hold all the power in a country?
  5. Is it important to read books whose ideas you think are wrong? Why?

About ages 8 to 12. Read it together, or on your own.

Karl Marx spent years in a great London library, reading reports about factories, money and work, and writing a giant book called Capital. He wanted to answer a question: where do the profits of a business come from?

Marx's answer was that profits come from the workers. He said workers make more value in a day than they are paid for, and the owner keeps the extra. Most economists since then have disagreed and explain wages and profits in other ways, but his book made many people pay attention to how hard factory work was in the 1800s, when people, even children, often worked twelve hours or more.

blocks.name: gb-workday
blocks.cap: Marx's picture of a working day. Move the sliders to see his idea of "surplus" hours.

blocks.html:
🧩 Try this

Lemonade economics. Imagine a lemonade stand. List everything it needs: lemons, sugar, cups, a table, a sign, someone to make and sell it, someone who had the idea and took the risk. Where do you think the profit comes from? Is it fair for each person to share it the same way?

📖 For teens and adults

The full lesson.

Marx (1818–1883), with Engels the co-author of the Communist Manifesto, settled in London in 1849 as a refugee. Supported largely by Engels, he worked for years in the reading room of the British Museum on a critique of the economists. Volume 1 of Capital: A Critique of Political Economy appeared in Hamburg in 1867; Engels assembled Volumes 2 and 3 from Marx's manuscripts after his death. The English translation by Samuel Moore and Edward Aveling, edited by Engels, came out in 1887.

A commodity has a use value (what it is good for) and an exchange value (what it trades for). Following the classical economists Adam Smith and David Ricardo, Marx holds a labor theory of value: what gives goods their exchange value is the labor time socially necessary to make them.

Where does the extra in M–C–M′ come from, if goods trade at their value? Marx's answer: the worker sells his labor power, his capacity to work, for a wage that covers what he needs to live. But in a working day he can produce more value than that wage. The difference Marx calls surplus value, the source, in his theory, of profit.

blocks.name: gb-workday
blocks.cap: Marx's working day, in his terms, with his rate of surplus value.

blocks.title: Marx's rate of surplus value
blocks.q: A 12-hour day in which 6 hours of labor cover the wage. What is Marx's rate of surplus value?

blocks.text: The working day and the factory

blocks.html: The long middle of Volume 1 uses the reports of British factory inspectors to describe working conditions in the 1860s: very long hours, child labor, dangerous machines. Marx describes the fight over the Factory Acts, which limited hours, as a struggle over surplus value. Historians still value these chapters as a record of industrial life.

In the 1870s William Stanley Jevons, Carl Menger and Léon Walras independently developed marginal utility: the value of a thing depends on how useful one more unit is to people, not on the labor it took. Most economists since then reject the labor theory of value, and with it Marx's account of profit, explaining wages and profits instead by supply and demand for labor and capital, risk, and the value each adds. Critics such as Eugen von Böhm-Bawerk (1896) pointed to contradictions between Volumes 1 and 3. Marx's predictions that profits would fall and workers grow poorer did not come true in industrial countries. Marxist economists have offered replies, and the book remains much studied in the history of economic thought, sociology and history.

Treating Capital's theory of value as settled economics. It is a 19th-century theory, built on Ricardo, that most economists have replaced; its descriptions of 1860s factories are another matter, and are widely accepted.

🔭 Going deeper

Context, the big questions, and how later books answered.

items: Adam Smith's Wealth of Nations (earlier on this ladder) is the book Marx answers most often: the division of labor, wages, profit and the market.
Hegel: Marx said Hegel's method stood on its head and had to be "turned right side up," with material life first.
Aristotle's Politics had already distinguished using a thing from trading it, and questioned money made from money; Marx cites him.
Dickens, later in this era, shows the same London of debt, poverty and grinding work in fiction.
What makes something valuable: the work that went into it, or how much people want it?
Who should share in a business's profits, and on what basis?
Why did working hours fall over the last two centuries?
What can a theory get right in its descriptions even if its explanations are wrong?

blocks.html: For the economics, see the Economics Ladder's topics on economic systems, supply and labor markets.

💬 Talk about it together

  1. Where do you think a business's profits come from?
  2. Is a thing worth what it took to make, or what people will pay? Can you think of examples both ways?
  3. Children in the 1860s often worked in factories. What protects children today?
  4. Why might a book matter in history even if many of its ideas turned out wrong?
  5. What would a fair working day look like to you?

About ages 8 to 12. Read it together, or on your own.

Michael Faraday was born in London in 1791. His family was poor, and he left school at 13 to work for a bookbinder. While he sewed books together, he read them, especially the ones about science. He went to hear a famous chemist, Humphry Davy, give lectures, wrote out neat notes, and sent them to Davy. Davy gave him a job as his helper.

Scientists already knew that electricity flowing in a wire makes it act like a magnet. Faraday asked the opposite question: can a magnet make electricity? He tried for years. In 1831 he found the answer. A magnet sitting still inside a coil of wire does nothing. But when he pushed the magnet in or pulled it out, a needle on his meter jumped. A moving magnet makes electricity flow!

blocks.name: gb-faraday-induction
blocks.cap: Push the magnet in and pull it out. The meter only moves while the magnet is moving, and it swings the other way when you pull it out.

blocks.html: That discovery runs our world. Almost all the electricity in your house is made in power stations by spinning magnets and coils of wire, just as Faraday found.

Faraday also loved teaching children. Every Christmas he gave lectures for young people at the Royal Institution in London. The most famous ones are about a single candle: what it is made of, why the flame has its shape, and where the wax goes when it burns.

🧩 Try this

Watch a candle like Faraday. With a grown-up, light a candle on a plate. Look closely: where is the flame brightest? Is there a dark part near the wick? Hold a cold metal spoon high above the flame for a moment. What forms on it? (Faraday showed that a burning candle makes water.) Read his lectures together in our Chemical History of a Candle course.

📖 For teens and adults

The full lesson.

Michael Faraday (1791–1867) was the son of a London blacksmith. He was apprenticed to a bookbinder at 14 and taught himself science from the books he bound. In 1813 Humphry Davy hired him as an assistant at the Royal Institution, where Faraday worked for the rest of his life, becoming its director of the laboratory and its most famous lecturer. He had almost no mathematical training. His Experimental Researches in Electricity are 30 series of papers sent to the Royal Society from 1831 to 1855, each with numbered paragraphs, collected into three volumes (1839, 1844 and 1855).

The problem: in 1820 Hans Christian Ørsted found that an electric current turns a compass needle, so electricity can make magnetism. Many people suspected the reverse must also be true, that magnetism could make electricity, but experiment after experiment failed. A strong magnet next to a wire did nothing.

items: Electromagnetic induction (1831). A changing magnetic effect makes a current. Switching a current on or off in one coil makes a brief current in a second coil wound on the same iron ring. Moving a magnet into or out of a coil does the same.
The first generator. A copper disk spinning between the poles of a magnet gives a steady current (October 1831).
One electricity. Current from batteries, from friction, from magnets, from electric fish and from heat are all the same thing (Third Series, 1833).

The laws of electrolysis (1833–1834). The amount of a substance freed by a current is in proportion to the amount of electricity passed. With the scholar William Whewell he made up the words electrode, anode, cathode, ion and electrolyte.

Lines of force and fields. Faraday pictured the space around magnets and currents as filled with curved "lines of force," which iron filings make visible. The forces live in the space, not only in the objects. This is the beginning of the idea of a field.
Light and magnetism (1845). A magnet can turn the plane of polarized light passing through heavy glass (the Faraday effect), a first sign that light is linked to electricity and magnetism.

blocks.html: This is the key: nothing happens while the current is steady. Only the change, switching on or switching off, induces a current, and the two kicks go in opposite directions.

blocks.name: gb-faraday-induction
blocks.cap: Faraday's paragraph 39 as a simulation. Drag the magnet or press the buttons. The meter shows the induced voltage, which depends on how fast the magnetic flux through the coil changes and on the number of turns.

blocks.html: In modern form, Faraday's law says the voltage induced in a coil is $\mathcal{E} = -N\dfrac{\Delta\Phi}{\Delta t}$: the number of turns times the rate of change of the magnetic flux $\Phi = BA$ through each turn. The minus sign (Lenz's law, 1834) says the induced current pushes back against the change.

blocks.title: A magnet into a coil
blocks.q: A coil of 200 turns, each of area $0.0030\ \text{m}^2$. A magnet is pushed in, raising the field through the coil from 0 to 0.25 T in 0.10 s. What average voltage is induced?
steps: Change of flux per turn: $\Delta\Phi = 0.25 \times 0.0030 = 7.5\times10^{-4}$ Wb.
blocks.a: 1.5 volts on average, about one flashlight battery. Push twice as fast and you get twice the voltage.

blocks.title: Faraday's ring as a transformer
blocks.q: Faraday's iron ring had two coils. Today's transformers are the same idea: $V_2/V_1 = N_2/N_1$ for an alternating current. A transformer steps 240 V down with 1,200 turns on the first coil and 60 on the second. What is the output?

blocks.title: Electrolysis
blocks.q: A current of 2.0 A passes through copper sulfate solution for 30 minutes. How much copper (molar mass 63.5 g/mol, charge 2+) is deposited? Use 96,500 C for one mole of electrons.
steps: Copper needs 2 electrons per atom: $0.0373/2 = 0.01865$ mol, times 63.5 g/mol $\approx 1.18$ g.
blocks.a: About 1.18 g. The constant 96,485 C/mol is named the faraday.

blocks.html: Faraday founded the Royal Institution's Christmas Lectures for young people in 1825 and gave nineteen series of them. The Chemical History of a Candle (lectures of 1860–1861, printed in 1861) follows a single candle into the chemistry of burning, the makeup of air and water, and our own breathing. Two of his popular lectures, on gravitation and on magnetism and electricity, from The Forces of Matter, are Harvard Classics readings.

items: Joseph Henry, too. The American Joseph Henry found induction independently at about the same time and also discovered self-induction, but Faraday published first, in November 1831. The unit of inductance, the henry, honors him.

Faraday did not invent the electric power industry by himself. His disk and his coils were laboratory devices that made tiny currents. Practical generators (from Hippolyte Pixii's in 1832 onward), transformers and power stations took the work of many engineers over the next 50 years.

No math, but not no theory. Faraday's papers contain almost no equations, but they are full of careful reasoning about lines of force. James Clerk Maxwell wrote that he found Faraday's way of thinking to be mathematical in a deep sense, and turned it into equations.

blocks.text: What later science kept, and what it changed

items: Kept: induction, the laws of electrolysis, the motor and generator principles, the Faraday effect and the words he coined. Faraday's law is one of Maxwell's four equations.

Built on: Maxwell turned lines of force into the mathematics of fields (1855–1865) and found that light is an electromagnetic wave, as Faraday had guessed. Heinrich Hertz made such waves in 1887: radio.
Changed: Faraday hoped gravity too would be linked to electricity and magnetism and searched for it without success. Gravity is still described separately, by Einstein's general relativity.

blocks.html:
🔭 Going deeper

Context, the big questions, and how later books answered.

Fields, not forces at a distance. Newton had said he framed no hypotheses about how gravity reaches across space. Faraday's answer for electricity and magnetism was that the space itself carries the action: lines of force with real physical existence. In his 1846 lecture "Thoughts on Ray-Vibrations" he even suggested that light might be a vibration of those lines. Maxwell, Einstein and modern physics all think in terms of fields.

A notebook science. Faraday's laboratory diary runs to thousands of numbered entries. The Researches keep the same numbering, so he can refer back to an earlier paragraph like a proof refers to an earlier theorem. They are a rare chance to watch a great experimenter think, try, fail and try again.

Faith and science. Faraday was a lifelong member and elder of a small Christian church, the Sandemanians. He saw the laws of nature as a reflection of the order of creation, and kept his faith and his laboratory work as separate kinds of activity. Historians have discussed how his belief in the unity of nature's forces may have guided his search for links between them.

Teaching. Faraday's advice to lecturers was to show experiments, speak plainly and treat the audience as friends. His Christmas Lectures, still given every year at the Royal Institution, are a model for anyone who explains science to young people.
End of the science shelf. Faraday is the last scientist in volume 42 of the set. The next science on the ladder, Darwin (volume 49), turns from physics and chemistry to the history of life.

💬 Talk about it together

  1. Faraday left school at 13 and became one of the greatest scientists. What helped him? What can you learn on your own?
  2. Nothing happened when the magnet sat still inside the coil. Why do you think change was the key?
  3. Joseph Henry found induction at about the same time. Should both men share the credit? How do we decide?
  4. Faraday used almost no math, and Maxwell turned his ideas into equations. Do pictures and words or equations help you understand better?
  5. Faraday chose a candle to teach children about all of science. If you had to teach someone science with one everyday object, what would you choose?
  6. Faraday kept his faith and his science as separate activities, yet thought both pointed to order in nature. How do the people you know think about science and belief?

When Charles Darwin was 22, he sailed around the world on a ship called the Beagle. For five years he collected beetles, birds, fossils and plants. On the Galápagos Islands he noticed that each island had its own kinds of finches and tortoises, a little different from the next island's.
Back home in England he wondered why. After twenty years of thinking and experimenting, he wrote On the Origin of Species (1859). His big idea, natural selection, goes like this:

items: Living things are all a little different, even brothers and sisters.
Many of those differences are passed on to the young.
More young are born than can possibly survive.
The ones whose differences help them live are more likely to grow up and have young of their own.
Over a very long time, these small changes add up, and new kinds of living things appear.

blocks.name: gb-selection
blocks.cap: Birds catch the beetles they can see. Press Next generation a few times. Then switch the ground.

blocks.html:
🧩 Try this

Hide the beans. Spread a handful of light and dark dried beans (or paper dots) on a dark towel. Give a family member ten seconds to pick up as many as they can. Which color was left? Now try on a light towel.

Darwin's own nature table: he loved simple experiments, like counting seedlings in a patch of ground he had cleared, or floating seeds in salt water to see if they could cross the sea. You can try both.

📖 For teens and adults

The full lesson.

Charles Darwin (1809–1882), grandson of the physician-poet Erasmus Darwin and of the potter Josiah Wedgwood, studied medicine at Edinburgh and then trained for the church at Cambridge, where he fell in love with natural history. From 1831 to 1836 he sailed as naturalist on HMS Beagle, reading Charles Lyell's Principles of Geology on the way. In 1838 he read Thomas Malthus on population and saw how selection could work. He wrote sketches of his theory in 1842 and 1844 but held back for years, gathering evidence. In 1858 Alfred Russel Wallace, working in the Malay islands, sent him an essay with the same idea; their papers were presented together that July, and Darwin hurried out the Origin, published November 24, 1859.

Darwin called the book "one long argument." It starts with what breeders of pigeons, dogs and crops already knew: by choosing which animals have young, they change a breed a great deal in a few generations. Then comes the struggle for existence: every species produces far more young than can survive.

blocks.title: Darwin's doubling plants
blocks.q: Darwin imagined an annual plant making only two seeds a year, all of which grew. Starting from one plant, how many after 20 years?
blocks.a: About a million plants, so most seeds in nature must fail to grow up.

blocks.name: gb-selection
blocks.cap: A simple model: the population changes because some kinds survive and breed more.

blocks.html: Darwin piles up evidence: the fossil record, the way species are spread across the globe (island species resemble those of the nearest mainland), the shared body plans of very different animals, and embryos. He also faces his "difficulties on theory" head-on: how could an organ as complex as the eye arise by small steps? Why are there gaps in the fossil record? He answers each in turn, and admits what he cannot yet explain.

Darwin's theory has two parts. Descent with modification: all living things are related, descended from common ancestors. Natural selection: the main way they change. Darwin saw life as a branching tree; the book's only illustration is a branching diagram.

Darwin did not know how inheritance works; his own guess was wrong. Gregor Mendel's experiments with peas (1866) were rediscovered in 1900, and in the 1930s and 1940s biologists joined genetics and natural selection in the "modern synthesis." DNA, fossils found since, and observed cases of evolution, such as bacteria becoming resistant to antibiotics, have confirmed descent with modification. Evolution by natural selection is the foundation of modern biology, though scientists still study how much other forces, such as chance drift, contribute.

The book also raised religious questions. Some readers saw it as a threat to faith; others, such as the American botanist Asa Gray, Darwin's friend, saw no conflict between evolution and belief in a Creator. Darwin himself described his views late in life as agnostic. Readers today still hold a range of views on how science and faith fit together.
Thinking individuals evolve. In natural selection no single animal changes its traits; the makeup of the population changes over generations.

🔭 Going deeper

Context, the big questions, and how later books answered.

items: Aristotle's biology, earlier on this ladder, had classified animals by fixed kinds; Darwin made the kinds themselves change.
Lucretius imagined creatures that failed to survive in a world of atoms, a distant ancestor of the idea.
Malthus and Adam Smith: ideas of population and competition from economics helped Darwin see nature's economy.
The Descent of Man, Darwin's next rung, applies the theory to human beings.
How can small changes add up to something entirely new?
What counts as good evidence for something that happened over millions of years?
Why did Darwin wait twenty years to publish?
Do science and faith answer the same questions, or different ones?

💬 Talk about it together

  1. What differences can you see among the people, pets or plants in your home?
  2. Why do you think Darwin spent so long collecting evidence before he published?
  3. What animal do you know that is well hidden in its home? How might that have come about?
  4. Darwin and Wallace had the same idea at the same time. How do you think they handled it fairly?
  5. Darwin said there is grandeur in this view of life. What do you find wonderful about living things?

🌱 For young readers

About ages 8 to 12. Read it together, or on your own.

In his first big book, Darwin said almost nothing about people. Twelve years later, in The Descent of Man (1871), he asked: do human beings belong to the same great family tree as every other living thing? His answer was yes.

Darwin pointed out that our bodies share the same plan as other animals'. Look at the bones in your arm. A bat's wing, a whale's flipper and a bird's wing have the same bones, in the same order, shaped for different jobs.

blocks.name: gb-homology
blocks.cap: The same bones in four very different limbs. Tap each group to light it up.

blocks.html: Darwin also wrote about why so many animals are colorful or sing: a peacock's huge tail or a songbird's tune help them win a mate. He called this sexual selection, which simply means traits that help animals be chosen as partners.

For parents: Darwin's book also contains Victorian opinions about different peoples and about women that science has since shown to be wrong. The lesson says so plainly. The chapters on animals (beetles, birds, butterflies) are the best place for young readers.

🧩 Try this

Feel your bones. Gently press along your arm: one long bone above the elbow, two bones from elbow to wrist (turn your hand over and feel them move), a knobby wrist, then finger bones. Now look at a picture of a bat's wing. Can you find the same parts?

📖 For teens and adults

The full lesson.

In the Origin (1859) Darwin wrote only one sentence about our own species: "Light will be thrown on the origin of man and his history." He knew the subject would cause a storm. By 1871, when The Descent of Man, and Selection in Relation to Sex appeared in two volumes, Thomas Henry Huxley and others had already argued in public for human evolution, and Darwin felt ready to give his evidence.

Part I gathers the evidence that humans descend, with other primates, from common ancestors: the same bone plan in our arms as in other mammals' limbs; embryos that look alike early on; and "rudimentary" organs that seem left over from ancestors, such as the small muscles some people can use to wiggle their ears. Darwin argued that humans and apes share ancestors; he did not claim that we descend from any living ape. He suggested that Africa was the likeliest birthplace of humanity, a guess that fossils and DNA have since supported.

blocks.name: gb-homology
blocks.cap: Homology: one plan of bones, four different jobs.

blocks.text: The mind and the moral sense

blocks.html: The boldest chapters argue that human mental powers, even conscience, differ from those of other animals in degree, not in kind. Darwin thought the moral sense grew from social instincts and sympathy, strengthened by language, habit, reason and teaching.

More than half the book is about sexual selection in animals, from beetles to birds of paradise. Some traits spread not because they help an animal survive but because they help it win mates: through rivalry, as with a stag's antlers, or through choice, as with a peacock's tail. Many biologists of Darwin's day doubted that females chose mates; today sexual selection is a major field of study, and much of Darwin's account has been confirmed.

The book reflects the prejudices of Victorian England. Darwin argued that all human beings belong to one species and he hated slavery, which he had seen in Brazil. But he also ranked human groups by ability and called women naturally less able than men in intellect. Modern science rejects both: genetic differences among human populations are small and do not form a ranking, and differences in achievement between groups and between the sexes have been shown to depend heavily on education and opportunity. Some later writers also misused Darwin's ideas to support "social Darwinism" and the eugenics movement, causes that brought great harm and that biologists today reject.
Saying Darwin claimed "humans came from monkeys." He argued that humans and the other primates share common ancestors, like cousins with shared great-grandparents.

🔭 Going deeper

Context, the big questions, and how later books answered.

blocks.text: The Descent in the great conversation

items: Aristotle placed humans at the top of the animals as the rational animal; Darwin kept humans among the animals but traced reason itself to natural causes.
Wallace, co-discoverer of natural selection, broke with Darwin here, doubting that selection alone could explain the human mind.
Freud and William James, later on this ladder, built their psychologies on the idea that humans are evolved animals.
Nietzsche asked what becomes of morality once its natural history is known.
Is conscience something only humans have? What do animals show of kindness or fairness?
How can a great scientist be right about the big picture and wrong about some of his own society's prejudices?
Why is it important not to use science to rank groups of people?
What does it mean to be related to every other living thing?

  1. What do you think makes humans different from other animals? What makes us alike?
  2. Darwin thought caring for others is the most noble thing about people. Do you agree?
  3. Why do you think many birds and animals are so colorful?
  4. Darwin was wrong about some groups of people. Why is it important to say so clearly?
  5. How would you feel about being cousin to every living thing?

🌱 For young readers

About ages 8 to 12. Read it together, or on your own.
William James was a Harvard professor and one of the first people to study the mind as a science. He wanted to know: how do we pay attention? How do habits form? What is a feeling?
James noticed that your thoughts never stop. They flow from one thing to the next, like a river. He called this the stream of consciousness.

He also noticed that the more you do something, the easier it gets, like a path through grass that gets clearer each time you walk it. That is a habit. Good habits, he said, are worth building early, because they make life easier for years.

blocks.name: gb-james-habit
blocks.cap: Move the slider: each repetition wears the path deeper and the task takes less effort. (A picture of the idea, not real measurements.)

blocks.html:
🧩 Try this

A habit experiment. Choose one small good habit, like putting your shoes in the same place or reading five minutes before bed. Do it every day for two weeks and mark a calendar. James had a rule: do not skip, especially at first. Was it easier by the end?

📖 For teens and adults

The full lesson.

William James (1842–1910), elder brother of the novelist Henry James, studied painting and then medicine, and in 1872 began teaching anatomy and physiology at Harvard. He set up one of the first teaching laboratories for psychology in the 1870s, and in 1878 agreed to write a textbook. It took twelve years. The Principles of Psychology (1890), in two volumes and about 1,400 pages, mixed physiology, laboratory findings, careful self-observation and lively writing. A shorter version followed in 1892. James later turned to philosophy and religion, becoming a founder of pragmatism and writing The Varieties of Religious Experience (1902).

James begins with the brain and the nervous system, and soon comes to habit. Living matter, he says, is plastic: it can be shaped, and once shaped it keeps the form, like a fold in paper. So repeated actions become easier, more exact, and need less attention.

He gives practical rules (our summary): start a new habit with as strong a beginning as possible; never allow an exception until it is firmly rooted; act on every good resolution at the first chance; and keep the power of effort alive with a little unneeded effort each day.

blocks.name: gb-james-habit
blocks.cap: An illustration of James's picture of habit.

blocks.html: Thought, James says, is always personal, always changing, continuous, and always about something, and it is always choosing, attending to some things and ignoring others. Novelists such as Virginia Woolf and James Joyce later took up "stream of consciousness" as a way of writing.

James's most surprising idea turns common sense around. We usually think we see a bear, feel afraid, and then run. James argued that the body reacts first, and the emotion is our feeling of those bodily changes. The Danish physician Carl Lange reached a similar idea at about the same time, so it is called the James-Lange theory.

blocks.name: gb-james-emotion
blocks.cap: Switch between common sense and James's order.

blocks.html: Much of James has lasted. Research on skills and the brain supports his picture of habit becoming automatic with practice; his account of attention as limited and selective set the questions for a century of experiments. His theory of emotion was challenged by the physiologist Walter Cannon in 1927, who argued that bodily changes are too slow and too similar to tell emotions apart; later studies found that the body's state does shape feeling, but that how we interpret a situation matters too, so most psychologists today hold mixed views. Some of the Principles, such as its physiology, is simply out of date. In his shorter textbook of 1892 James called psychology "only the hope of a science," a modest view that helped keep the field open to evidence.
Thinking James was only a laboratory scientist. He trusted careful self-observation as much as experiments, and he wrote as much about free will, the self and religious experience as about nerves.

🔭 Going deeper

Context, the big questions, and how later books answered.

items: Aristotle's On the Soul and Locke's Essay, earlier on this ladder, also asked how experience builds the mind; James replaced Locke's separate "ideas" with a flowing stream.
Darwin taught James to see the mind as an evolved tool for survival, and habits and instincts as part of our animal inheritance.
Freud, the next great psychologist on this ladder, explored the parts of the mind outside awareness that James also wrote about.
The Memory Ladder's topics on attention and long-term memory take up questions James raised.
Do you control your habits, or do your habits control you?
Can you notice your own stream of thoughts without changing it?
Do you smile because you are happy, or can smiling make you happier?
Why is paying attention a kind of choice?

blocks.html:
💬 Talk about it together

  1. What is a good habit someone in your family has? How did they build it?
  2. Try to notice your thoughts for one minute. Where did they wander?
  3. When you are scared, what happens in your body first?
  4. What makes it hard to pay attention? What helps?
  5. James said to act on a good resolution right away. Why might waiting make it harder?
