About ages 8 to 12. Read it together, or on your own.
Johann Wolfgang von Goethe (say GUR-tuh) was Germany's most famous poet. He worked on one play, Faust, for about sixty years, from when he was a young man until just before he died.

Faust is a scholar who has read every book in his study and still feels he knows nothing important. A clever devil named Mephistopheles (say meff-ih-STOFF-uh-leez) offers him a deal: he will show Faust every pleasure in the world. Faust makes a bet: if he ever finds a moment so wonderful that he wants it to last forever, he will lose.

Faust goes on many adventures, makes terrible mistakes, and hurts people he loves. But he keeps striving, and at the very end he finds his happiest moment not in pleasure but in planning work that will help many people live freely. And, in Goethe's version, he is saved.

blocks.name: gb-faust-journey
blocks.cap: Faust's journey, scene by scene. Switch between Part One and Part Two.

blocks.html: For parents: Part One includes the tragedy of Gretchen, which involves adult themes. The lesson summarizes it gently. Young readers can enjoy the opening scenes and the idea of the wager, or a retelling.

🧩 Try this

The moment you'd keep. Faust is looking for one perfect moment. Draw or write about a moment you wish could have lasted forever. What made it special? Was it something you got, or something you did or shared?

📖 For teens and adults

The full lesson.

Goethe (1749–1832) was a poet, novelist, scientist and statesman at the small court of Weimar. The Faust legend, a German tale of a scholar who sells his soul for knowledge and power, was already old; Christopher Marlowe had made it a play in the 1590s, and Goethe saw it as a puppet show as a boy. He began his own version in the 1770s, published Part One in 1808, and finished Part Two in 1831; it appeared in 1832, after his death. Bayard Taylor's English translation (1870–71) keeps Goethe's rhymes and meters.

The play opens with a Prologue in Heaven, modeled on the Book of Job: Mephistopheles asks to tempt Faust, and the Lord allows it, confident that "a good man, through obscurest aspiration, / Has still an instinct of the one true way." Faust, in despair, turns to magic, and Mephistopheles comes to him, first as a black poodle.

The wager changes the old legend. Marlowe's Faustus sells his soul for twenty-four years of power. Goethe's Faust bets that nothing Mephistopheles offers will ever satisfy his restless striving. The question of the play is whether striving itself is Faust's curse or his salvation.

blocks.name: gb-faust-journey
blocks.cap: Our summaries of the main scenes.

blocks.html: The heart of Part One is the story of Gretchen (Margaret), a pious young townswoman whom Faust loves and, with Mephistopheles' help, pursues. Their love brings ruin on her family, and she is condemned for a terrible act done in despair. In the last scene Faust tries to rescue her from prison; she refuses to escape with him and gives herself to God's judgment. Mephistopheles cries that she is judged; a voice from above answers, "She is saved."

blocks.name: gb-faust-journey
blocks.cap: Part Two: the court, Helen, the land from the sea and Faust's rescue.

blocks.html: Part Two is a vast symbolic pageant through politics, money, ancient Greece and science. At the end, old and blind, Faust plans to drain a marsh so that free people can live on new land. Imagining that, he says the fatal words and dies. But angels carry off his immortal part, singing:

Thinking Faust is simply a warning against ambition. Goethe's play judges Faust harshly for the harm he does, yet ends in mercy for a man who never stopped striving. Readers still argue about whether that ending is just.

🔭 Going deeper

Context, the big questions, and how later books answered.

items: The Book of Job and Dante's Comedy: Goethe's Prologue echoes Job, and his ending, with Gretchen among the blessed leading Faust upward, echoes Beatrice in the Paradiso.
Marlowe's Doctor Faustus (1590s) ends in damnation; Goethe's ends in redemption.
Milton's Satan and Goethe's Mephistopheles are two great portraits of evil, one grand, one witty and mocking.
Later, "Faustian" became a word for a restless hunger for knowledge and power at any cost.
Is never being satisfied a good thing or a bad thing?
Can someone who does great harm still be forgiven? Who decides?
Why does the devil say he "works the Good" without meaning to?
What kind of moment would truly be worth asking to stay?

blocks.html:
💬 Talk about it together

  1. Faust read every book and still felt empty. What do you think he was missing?
  2. Why do you think Goethe let Faust be saved, when the old story ended in punishment?
  3. Is it ever wise to make a bet about your own happiness?
  4. Faust's happiest moment came from planning work that helps others. Why might that be more satisfying than fun?
  5. What would you warn Faust about, if you could talk to him at the start?

About ages 8 to 12. Read it together, or on your own.
Jane Austen wrote six famous novels in England about 200 years ago. Emma is about a clever, kind-hearted, rather bossy young woman named Emma Woodhouse who loves playing matchmaker in her village.

There is just one problem: Emma is almost always wrong. She thinks the vicar loves her friend Harriet, but he really wants to marry Emma. She thinks a charming young man is in love with her, but he has a secret. And she never notices who really cares about her.

blocks.name: gb-emma-matches
blocks.cap: Switch between Emma's plans and what really happens. Tap a name to read about each person.

blocks.html: Along the way Emma makes a hurtful joke about a poor, kind older woman, and her friend Mr. Knightley tells her plainly that it was wrong. Emma feels terrible, and she changes. The book is funny, but it is also about learning to see other people truly and to be kind.

🧩 Try this

Match the clues. Emma jumped to conclusions. Play a detective game: one person acts out a short scene without words (for example, looking for lost keys), and everyone guesses what is going on. Was the first guess right? What clue did people miss?

📖 For teens and adults

The full lesson.

Jane Austen (1775–1817), a clergyman's daughter, lived most of her life in country villages in the south of England. She published four novels in her lifetime, all anonymously, "By the Author of Pride and Prejudice" and so on; two more appeared after her death. Emma came out in December 1815 (dated 1816), dedicated, at his request, to the Prince Regent, who admired her books. She reportedly said she was creating a heroine whom no one but herself would much like.
Notice the word seemed. The opening sentence already hints that Emma's comfortable life will be tested.

Emma has just seen her governess, Miss Taylor, marry the widower Mr. Weston, and she takes credit for the match. Bored, she adopts a sweet young friend, Harriet Smith, and persuades her to refuse a good farmer, Robert Martin, so that she can marry the vicar, Mr. Elton. Mr. Elton, it turns out, wants Emma. Then Frank Churchill, Mr. Weston's charming son, arrives and flirts with Emma, while the quiet, gifted Jane Fairfax keeps her distance. Emma misreads everyone.

blocks.name: gb-emma-matches
blocks.cap: Our map of Highbury: Emma's plans, then what really happens.

blocks.html: At a picnic on Box Hill, Emma makes a joke at the expense of Miss Bates, a poor, good-natured, endlessly talkative older woman. Afterward Mr. Knightley takes her aside:

Emma cries all the way home, and the next morning she visits Miss Bates to make amends. Soon the secrets come out: Frank has been engaged to Jane all along, and when Harriet confesses that she hopes Mr. Knightley loves her, Emma realizes, in a flash, that she loves him herself.

Austen tells the story mostly through Emma's own thoughts, in a style later called free indirect discourse: the narrator's voice slips into the character's way of seeing. So readers make Emma's mistakes along with her, and learn as she learns.
Reading Emma as only a romance. It is a comedy about judgment: how pride, boredom and wishful thinking lead a clever person to see what she wants to see.

🔭 Going deeper

Context, the big questions, and how later books answered.

items: Aristotle's Ethics, earlier on this ladder, says we become good by practice and correct our faults through friends who tell us the truth; Mr. Knightley is that kind of friend.
Shakespeare's comedies, such as Much Ado About Nothing, also turn on misreadings and matchmaking.
George Eliot's Middlemarch, later in this era, widens Austen's village into a whole town and its web of lives.
Sir Walter Scott, reviewing Emma in 1815–16, praised Austen for making ordinary life interesting.
Why is it so easy to see what we want to see?
What makes a good friend: someone who agrees with you, or someone who tells you the truth?
Is it ever right to arrange other people's lives for them?
How should we treat people who have less money or status than we do?

blocks.html:
💬 Talk about it together

  1. Have you ever been sure about something and then found out you were wrong?
  2. Mr. Knightley told Emma a hard truth. Is that kind or unkind? Why?
  3. Why do you think Emma made fun of Miss Bates? How did she make it right?
  4. Is it a good idea to try to choose friends or partners for other people?
  5. Which character in Emma would you most like to meet?

🌱 For young readers

About ages 8 to 12. Read it together, or on your own.
For parents: Cousin Bette is a novel for adults, about grown-ups' bad choices, broken promises and ruin. The young readers' path talks only about its main theme, envy, which children understand well.
Honoré de Balzac (say BAL-zak) was a French writer who drank huge amounts of coffee and wrote almost ninety novels about life in France. He wanted to describe a whole society, rich and poor.

Cousin Bette is about a poor cousin who smiles and helps her rich relatives, while secretly she is jealous of them, and her jealousy grows and grows until it causes great harm. Balzac shows how a small, hidden feeling can become dangerous if it is never faced.

blocks.name: gb-bette-family
blocks.cap: The two families at the center of the story. Tap a name.

blocks.html:
🧩 Try this

The green-eyed monster. Envy means wanting what someone else has and feeling bad that they have it. Talk together: when have you felt envy? What helped it go away? Make a list of three things to do instead of letting envy grow, like telling someone, counting your own good things, or being glad for the other person.

📖 For teens and adults

The full lesson.

Honoré de Balzac (1799–1850) wrote at a furious pace, often through the night, to pay off his debts. He gathered his novels and stories, around ninety in all, into one great series, The Human Comedy, in which characters reappear from book to book and together picture French society from peasants to bankers. Cousin Bette appeared as a newspaper serial in 1846; with Cousin Pons it forms a pair called Poor Relations. It is one of his last great novels.
Lisbeth Fischer, called Cousin Bette, comes from a peasant family in the Vosges. Her pretty cousin Adeline married a rising officer of Napoleon's army, Hector Hulot, who became a baron.

Bette has taken under her wing a young Polish sculptor in exile, Wenceslas Steinbock. When Adeline's daughter Hortense meets and marries him, Bette's buried envy turns into a plan for revenge. She allies herself with Valérie Marneffe, a scheming young wife who entangles Baron Hulot and the rich Crevel and drains their money. The baron's weakness leads him into debt, disgrace and the ruin of others. Through it all Adeline, patient and pious, keeps forgiving.

blocks.name: gb-bette-family
blocks.cap: Our map of who is who.

blocks.html: Balzac is a founder of literary realism. He describes rooms, clothes, debts and prices in great detail, because he believed people's money and surroundings shape their souls. Cousin Bette shows a society in which money and appearances rule, and in which hidden passions, envy most of all, do more harm than open crimes.

Readers have long argued about Balzac's view. Some see him as a moralist who shows vice destroying itself and goodness, in Adeline, enduring; others see a coolly scientific observer more interested in how passions work than in judging them. Balzac himself, in his foreword to the Human Comedy, compared himself to a naturalist classifying species.

Seeing Bette as a simple villain. Balzac makes us understand her: a lifetime of being overlooked, and pride that will not admit it. That does not excuse what she does, but it makes the book a study of how resentment grows.

🔭 Going deeper

Context, the big questions, and how later books answered.

items: Dante had already pictured envy as a sin that blinds; Balzac shows it working in a modern city.
Dickens and George Eliot, later in this era, also show families undone by money, debt and secrets.
Engels, Marx's partner, wrote that he learned more about French society from Balzac than from all the historians and economists.
Tolstoy and Dostoevsky carried Balzac's realism into Russia.
Why is hidden envy more dangerous than open anger?
Can understanding why someone does wrong be different from excusing it?
Is forgiveness like Adeline's always wise?
How much do money and surroundings shape a person's character?

blocks.html:
💬 Talk about it together

  1. What is the difference between envy and wanting to do well?
  2. Why do you think Bette hid her feelings for so long?
  3. Adeline forgave again and again. When is forgiving the right thing, and when does someone need to change first?
  4. How can a family make sure no one feels left out or less loved?
  5. Balzac described rooms and money in great detail. Why might that help tell a story?

Herman Melville went to sea as a young man and sailed on a whaling ship in the Pacific. Years later he wrote Moby-Dick, the story of a whaling voyage and a captain who will not give up.

A young man named Ishmael joins the crew of the ship Pequod with his new best friend, Queequeg, a harpooner from a far-off island. Their captain, Ahab, has a leg made of whalebone: on an earlier voyage, a giant white whale named Moby Dick took his leg. Now Ahab wants revenge, and he will chase the white whale around the world.

blocks.name: gb-pequod-voyage
blocks.cap: Follow the Pequod around the world, meeting other ships. Tap Next.

blocks.html: The book is also full of facts about whales: how big they are, how they swim, how sailors hunted them in the 1800s for the oil used in lamps. Melville loved whales, even while he wrote about hunting them.

For parents: the novel describes whaling, which was bloody work, and it ends in disaster for almost everyone aboard. Young readers enjoy the early chapters (Ishmael and Queequeg's friendship), the whale facts, and a good abridged edition.

🧩 Try this

How big is a whale? A large sperm whale like Moby Dick can be about 50 to 60 feet long. Go outside with a tape measure or count steps (one big step is about 3 feet). Mark out 55 feet. How many of your family lying head to toe would fit?

📖 For teens and adults

The full lesson.

Herman Melville (1819–1891) grew up in New York; when his family fell on hard times, he went to sea. In 1841 he sailed on the whaler Acushnet, jumped ship in the Marquesas, and returned home years later to write popular adventure books about the South Seas. Moby-Dick (1851), dedicated to his friend Nathaniel Hawthorne, was his most ambitious work. It sold poorly, and Melville died almost forgotten; in the 1920s critics rediscovered it, and it is now often called the great American novel.

Ishmael meets Queequeg at an inn in New Bedford, and the two become the closest of friends. They hear Father Mapple preach on Jonah and sign on the Pequod, which sails from Nantucket on Christmas Day. Captain Ahab stays out of sight until the ship is well at sea. Then, on the quarter-deck, he reveals the voyage's real purpose: to hunt down Moby Dick, the white whale that took his leg, and he nails a gold coin to the mast as a reward.

blocks.name: gb-pequod-voyage
blocks.cap: The voyage and the gams, the meetings with other ships.

blocks.html: The ship meets nine other ships at sea. Each gam brings news of Moby Dick and a different way of facing him: some captains have lost limbs or crew to the whale; one, the Rachel, is searching for its captain's lost son. Ahab will not stop for anyone.

Starbuck, the first mate, is brave but sensible; he begs Ahab to turn back, for the sake of the crew and their families. Ahab refuses. After three days of chase, the whale sinks the Pequod. Only Ishmael survives.

Between the adventures come chapters on whale anatomy, the classification of whales ("Cetology"), the whiteness of the whale, ropes, oil and paintings of whales. Melville mixes sermon, stage play, essay and science. Some readers skip these chapters; others think they are the book's heart, a way of showing that the whale, and the world, can never be fully known or caught.

Ahab sees in the white whale everything that has wounded and baffled him, and wants to strike back at it. Ishmael, the survivor, looks at the same world with curiosity, humor and friendship. The novel sets these two ways of living side by side.
Reading Moby-Dick as simply "man against nature." Ahab's real struggle is with his own pride and obsession, which drag his whole crew with him. Starbuck and Ishmael show other choices.

🔭 Going deeper

Context, the big questions, and how later books answered.

items: The Book of Jonah, retold in Father Mapple's sermon, and Job, whose Leviathan the whale recalls.
Shakespeare: Ahab speaks like a tragic hero, and some chapters are written as scenes from a play, with stage directions; Melville was reading King Lear and Macbeth.
Homer's Odyssey and Dante's Ulysses: voyages to the edge of the known world.
Darwin, in this same era, also looked closely at living things to ask what they mean; Melville's "Cetology" mocks and admires the classifiers.
When does determination turn into obsession?
Why do Ahab's crew follow him, even when they fear he is wrong?
What does the friendship of Ishmael and Queequeg show about prejudice?
Can a story be about one thing and everything at once?

blocks.html: See the Geography Ladder's topics on the world's oceans.

💬 Talk about it together

  1. What would you have done if you were Starbuck?
  2. Ishmael and Queequeg became friends even though they came from very different places. What helps people become friends?
  3. Ahab could not let go of his anger. Why is it hard to let go?
  4. Why do you think Melville put so many whale facts in a story?
  5. Is there something you would follow across the world?

Charles Dickens was the most popular writer in England in the 1800s. When he was twelve, his father was sent to a prison for people who could not pay their debts, and young Charles had to work in a factory pasting labels on bottles of shoe polish. He never forgot it.

In Little Dorrit, a girl named Amy Dorrit is born inside one of those prisons, the Marshalsea. She is small, quiet and very hardworking, and she takes care of her proud father and her whole family. A kind man named Arthur Clennam, just home from far away, wants to help her.

Dickens also makes fun of a government office that never gets anything done, the Circumlocution Office. (Circumlocution means "talking around and around.") Its whole skill, he jokes, is figuring out how not to do things.

blocks.name: gb-circumlocution
blocks.cap: Try to get an answer from the Circumlocution Office. Keep filing forms...

blocks.html:
🧩 Try this

Invent your own office. Dickens gave his office a silly name. Make up a pretend office that makes simple jobs hard, like the Department of Shoe-Tying, and write three of its rules. Then write one rule that would fix it.

📖 For teens and adults

The full lesson.

Charles Dickens (1812–1870) published his novels in monthly or weekly parts, read eagerly across Britain and America. In 1824 his father was imprisoned for debt in the Marshalsea prison in Southwark, and twelve-year-old Charles was sent to work in a blacking factory, a humiliation he kept secret for most of his life. Little Dorrit came out in monthly parts from December 1855 to June 1857, during years when Britain was angry about government bungling in the Crimean War.

The novel opens in a jail in Marseilles and moves to London, and nearly everyone in it is imprisoned in some way. William Dorrit has lived in the Marshalsea so long that he is called its "Father." His daughter Amy, born there, works quietly as a seamstress to keep the family going. Arthur Clennam, back from twenty years in China, returns to his mother's gloomy house, where she sits in a wheelchair, shut in by guilt and a hidden secret.

When Arthur tries to find out something simple about the Dorrits' debt, he is sent from office to office, form to form, by members of the Barnacle family, who cling to government jobs like barnacles to a ship. The inventor Daniel Doyce spends years trying to get anyone to look at his useful invention.

blocks.name: gb-circumlocution
blocks.cap: Our game version of the Circumlocution Office.

blocks.html: The book has two parts. In "Poverty," the Dorrits live in the prison. In "Riches," they suddenly inherit a fortune and tour Italy in grand style; William Dorrit, ashamed of his past, wants everyone to forget it, and Amy is lonelier than ever. Meanwhile all London worships the financier Mr. Merdle, until his empire is revealed as a fraud and collapses, ruining those who trusted him, Arthur among them. Arthur ends up in the Marshalsea himself, and Amy comes back to care for him.

Dickens's satire of red tape and of a financial bubble made the book controversial; some officials complained it was unfair. His deeper subject is how people imprison themselves, by pride, money or guilt, and how quiet goodness like Amy's sets them free.
Taking Dickens's comic exaggerations as exact history. The Circumlocution Office is invented; but debtors' prisons were real, and Parliament largely ended imprisonment for debt in England in 1869.

🔭 Going deeper

Context, the big questions, and how later books answered.

blocks.text: Little Dorrit in the great conversation

items: Dante and Milton pictured prisons of the soul; Dickens finds them in London streets.
Adam Smith and Marx, on this ladder, analyze money and credit; Dickens shows what a bubble does to people.
Balzac in France and Tolstoy in Russia also wrote of families undone or saved by money and pride.
Tocqueville and Mill worried about government that grows clumsy and self-serving; Dickens mocked it.
What kinds of invisible prisons can people live in?
Why is it so hard for a big organization to do simple things?
Does sudden wealth change people? How?
What makes someone like Little Dorrit strong, even though she is quiet?

blocks.html:
💬 Talk about it together

  1. Little Dorrit took care of her family when she was very young. What do you do to help your family?
  2. Have you ever had to go to many people to get one simple answer? How did it feel?
  3. Why do you think William Dorrit wanted to forget he had been in prison?
  4. Why do people trust someone like Mr. Merdle, who seems rich and important?
  5. The book ends with "a modest life of usefulness and happiness." What would that look like for you?

Leo Tolstoy was a Russian count who lived on a big country estate. He wrote one of the longest and most famous novels in the world, War and Peace, about Russian families living through the years when the French emperor Napoleon tried to conquer Russia.

We follow a kind, clumsy young man named Pierre; a brave, proud prince named Andrew; and a lively, warm-hearted girl named Natasha, along with their families. There are parties, dances, hunts, friendships, mistakes and, in 1812, a terrible war, when Napoleon's huge army marches all the way to Moscow.

blocks.name: gb-1812
blocks.cap: Follow Napoleon's army into Russia and back. Tap Next.

blocks.html: Tolstoy wondered: who really makes history? Is it emperors and generals, or millions of ordinary people each doing their part? He thought ordinary people matter much more than history books say.
For parents: the battle chapters describe the suffering of war plainly. Younger readers can enjoy the family chapters, such as Natasha's first ball and the wolf hunt, or a good abridgment.

🧩 Try this

History from below. Ask an older relative about an important event they lived through. What did they see, do or feel? Write it down. Tolstoy believed stories like theirs are the real history.

📖 For teens and adults

The full lesson.

Count Leo Tolstoy (1828–1910) served as an artillery officer in the Crimean War, then settled at his estate, Yasnaya Polyana, where he ran a school for peasant children. He wrote War and Peace between 1863 and 1869, with his wife Sophia copying out the drafts by hand. It appeared in parts from 1865 to 1869. Louise and Aylmer Maude, friends of Tolstoy, translated it into English in 1922–23.

The novel follows several families, above all the warm, impractical Rostovs (Natasha, her brother Nicholas, young Petya, their cousin Sonya), the proud Bolkonskys (Prince Andrew, his devout sister Princess Mary, their stern old father), and Pierre Bezukhov, the awkward illegitimate son who suddenly inherits a fortune. It runs from 1805, when Russia fights Napoleon in Austria, to 1812, when Napoleon invades Russia, and ends in 1820.
At the Battle of Austerlitz in 1805, Prince Andrew, dreaming of glory, falls wounded with a flag in his hands:

blocks.name: gb-1812
blocks.cap: Our sketch of the 1812 campaign as the novel follows it.

blocks.html: When Napoleon invades, the families scatter. At Borodino, Pierre wanders the battlefield and Andrew is wounded again; Moscow is abandoned and burns; Pierre, taken prisoner, meets the peasant soldier Platon Karataev, whose simple goodness changes him. In the long retreat the French army is destroyed by cold, hunger and pursuit. In the end Pierre marries Natasha, and Nicholas marries Princess Mary.

Tolstoy interrupts his story with essays arguing that Napoleon's genius was an illusion: battles and wars are decided by the countless choices of ordinary people, and great men only seem to lead. The old general Kutuzov, who waits and lets events unfold, is wiser than Napoleon, who thinks he commands them. The second Epilogue is a long essay on free will and necessity.

Readers argue about these essays. Many critics, and some historians, find Tolstoy's view too sweeping: leaders' decisions do sometimes change events. Others think he was right to turn attention to ordinary people. The philosopher Isaiah Berlin, in a famous 1953 essay, called Tolstoy a "fox" who saw many things but longed to be a "hedgehog" who knows one big thing.
Expecting a single hero. War and Peace has many centers; its real subject is life itself, in families, friendships and nations, and how people find meaning in it.

🔭 Going deeper

Context, the big questions, and how later books answered.

blocks.text: War and Peace in the great conversation

items: Homer's Iliad: Tolstoy saw himself writing a modern epic, with war seen from every side.
Hegel, earlier in this era, made "world-historical individuals" like Napoleon the agents of history; Tolstoy answers him directly.
Thucydides and Gibbon, earlier on this ladder, explain wars by leaders' decisions and causes; Tolstoy doubts such explanations.
Dostoevsky, the next Russian on this ladder, asked about faith and freedom in a darker key.
Do great leaders make history, or does history make them?
Where do people find meaning: in glory, in learning, in family, in faith?
Why might the most important changes in a life come in quiet moments, like Andrew's sky?
Can a person be both free and part of something much larger?

blocks.html:
💬 Talk about it together

  1. Which character would you most like to be friends with? Why?
  2. Prince Andrew wanted glory, then found peace looking at the sky. Have you ever changed your mind about what matters?
  3. Natasha gave the family's carts to wounded soldiers. What does that tell you about her?
  4. Tolstoy said ordinary people make history. What ordinary person do you admire?
  5. Why do you think Tolstoy called the book War and Peace?

George Eliot was really a woman named Mary Ann Evans. In her time, people did not always take women writers seriously, so she chose a man's name. Her novel Middlemarch is about a whole English town about 200 years ago, and the people in it, all connected like threads in a spider's web.

The main character, Dorothea, wants to do something great and good for the world. Things do not turn out the way she plans. But by the end, she does a great deal of good in quiet ways, helping the people around her. George Eliot says that's how much of the world's goodness happens: through people whose names never make it into history books.

blocks.name: gb-middlemarch-web
blocks.cap: The people of Middlemarch and how their stories touch. Tap a name.

blocks.html:
🧩 Try this

Unhistoric acts. George Eliot believed small kindnesses add up. For one week, keep a list of small good things you notice people doing: a neighbor helping, a sibling sharing, someone holding a door. At the end, read the list together. How many people did good without anyone noticing?

📖 For teens and adults

The full lesson.

Mary Ann Evans (1819–1880) grew up in the English Midlands, the daughter of a land agent. Deeply religious as a girl, she lost her faith in her twenties, translated German works of theology and philosophy, and became an editor of the Westminster Review in London. She took the pen name George Eliot for her novels, beginning in 1857. Middlemarch: A Study of Provincial Life appeared in eight parts in 1871–72 and is set in 1829–32, the years before the Reform Act of 1832.

blocks.name: gb-middlemarch-web
blocks.cap: Our map of the main characters.

items: Dorothea Brooke, ardent and idealistic, marries the elderly scholar Mr. Casaubon, hoping to share in his life's work, a "Key to all Mythologies." She finds him cold, jealous and lost in a project that will never be finished. After his death she gives up his fortune to marry his young cousin, Will Ladislaw.
Tertius Lydgate, a gifted young doctor, comes to town to reform medicine, marries the lovely, self-centered Rosamond Vincy, and is slowly worn down by debt and compromise.
Fred Vincy, Rosamond's idle brother, wins the sensible Mary Garth only after learning honest work from her father Caleb.
Mr. Bulstrode, the pious banker, hides a shameful past that comes back to destroy his standing, and nearly ruins Lydgate too.

blocks.html: Eliot's narrator often steps back to ask readers to understand even the least likable characters. Of Dorothea weeping on her honeymoon in Rome, she writes:

Eliot believed the novel's great work is to widen our sympathy: to help us feel that every other person has an inner life as real and complicated as our own. Even Casaubon, she insists, has his own "intense consciousness."
Reading Middlemarch as a story of failure. Most of its people do not achieve their dreams, but the novel honors the quieter good they do, and treats ordinary lives as worthy of the closest attention.

🔭 Going deeper

Context, the big questions, and how later books answered.

items: Austen, earlier in this era, drew a village; Eliot draws a whole town, with its banks, doctors, politics and gossip.
Aristotle and Kant asked what makes a life good; Eliot's answer is close to Aristotle's practical wisdom, lived among others.
Spinoza, whose Ethics Eliot translated into English (it was published only in 1981), shaped her calm, understanding view of human passions.
Tolstoy, later in this era, shares her belief that history is made by ordinary lives.
Is it better to aim for great deeds or to do small good things well?
How do small choices, like borrowing money or keeping a secret, shape a whole life?
Why is it hard to imagine that other people's inner lives are as real as ours?
What did Eliot mean by "unhistoric acts"?

blocks.html:
💬 Talk about it together

  1. Dorothea wanted to do something great. What great thing would you like to do? What small good thing could you do this week?
  2. Who in your life does good things quietly, without being noticed?
  3. Why do you think Mary Garth wanted Fred to have a useful job before she married him?
  4. George Eliot used a man's name to be taken seriously. How do you think that felt?
  5. Can you think of someone you didn't like at first and later understood better?

🌱 For young readers

About ages 8 to 12. Read it together, or on your own.
Henrik Ibsen was a playwright from Norway. Before him, most serious plays were about kings, gods and heroes. Ibsen wrote about ordinary families in ordinary living rooms, and the secrets they keep.

In his most famous play, A Doll's House, a young mother named Nora seems to have a perfect, cozy life. But she has a secret: years ago, when her husband was very sick, she borrowed money in secret to save him, and she broke a rule to do it. When the secret comes out, her husband cares more about what people will think than about her. Nora realizes she has been treated like a doll, and she decides she must learn to think for herself.

blocks.name: gb-ibsen-past
blocks.cap: In each play, a secret from the past comes out. Start with A Doll's House.

blocks.html: For parents: these are plays for older readers. A Doll's House is the best start for teens; the other three end in tragedy, which the lesson mentions without detail.

🧩 Try this

Act it out. A play is meant to be performed. With family members, act out a short scene where one person has to tell an important truth. How does each person feel? Try it two ways: the truth told gently, and blurted out. What changes?

📖 For teens and adults

The full lesson.

Henrik Ibsen (1828–1906) grew up in Skien, Norway, apprenticed to a pharmacist, and worked for years as a theater director in Bergen and Christiania (now Oslo). He then lived abroad, in Italy and Germany, from 1864 to 1891. After the great verse dramas Brand and Peer Gynt, he turned to prose plays set in middle-class homes. The Britannica set includes four: A Doll's House (1879), The Wild Duck (1884), Hedda Gabler (1890) and The Master Builder (1892). The Scottish critic William Archer translated and championed them in English.

Ibsen borrowed a technique from Greek tragedy, especially Oedipus: the most important events have already happened before the curtain rises. The play is the slow bringing to light of the past, and each revelation forces the characters to see themselves anew.

blocks.name: gb-ibsen-past
blocks.cap: Our summaries of the four plays: pick each one.

blocks.html: Nora Helmer seems a playful, pampered wife whom her husband Torvald calls his "little squirrel." Years ago she secretly borrowed money to save his life, forging her father's signature. When the lender, Krogstad, threatens to reveal it, Nora hopes for a "miracle": that Torvald will take the blame on himself. Instead he thinks only of his reputation. In the last scene she tells him she is leaving:

The slam of the door as Nora leaves shocked audiences across Europe; a German actress refused to play the ending, and Ibsen reluctantly wrote an alternative for that production. The play became central to debates about marriage and women's rights. Ibsen himself said he had written about the need for every person to become themselves, more than about any political cause.
The idealist Gregers Werle insists on telling his friend Hjalmar Ekdal the truth about his family's past, sure that truth will make their marriage nobler. The doctor Relling disagrees:

Gregers's truth breaks the family apart and ends in a heartbreaking tragedy. Readers still argue whether Ibsen is mocking his own earlier faith in truth-telling or warning about truth used without love.

blocks.text: Hedda Gabler and The Master Builder

blocks.html: Hedda Gabler is the portrait of a proud, bored woman who wants power over someone's fate and is trapped by her own choices. The Master Builder shows an aging architect, haunted by guilt over how his fortune began and afraid of the young, who climbs one last tower. Both end in tragedy.

Ibsen made the living room a place for tragedy. His characters speak everyday prose, yet each play asks a large question: what we owe ourselves, what we owe others, and when the truth heals or wounds.
Reading A Doll's House only as a pamphlet. Nora and Torvald are both people of their time; the play asks what a real marriage would require of both of them.

🔭 Going deeper

Context, the big questions, and how later books answered.

items: Sophocles' Oedipus, earlier on this ladder, gave Ibsen the shape of a play that uncovers the past.
Mill, in The Subjection of Women (1869), argued for women's equality in marriage; Ibsen's Nora dramatized such questions a decade later.
Kierkegaard, Ibsen's Scandinavian predecessor, also wrote about becoming oneself.
Later playwrights, from Chekhov to Arthur Miller, learned from his realism.
Is the truth always worth telling? When might it be kinder to wait, or to tell it differently?
What does it mean to become a person in your own right?
How do secrets from the past shape a family?
Why might a play about an ordinary home shock a whole continent?

blocks.html:
💬 Talk about it together

  1. Nora kept a secret to protect someone. Was that right?
  2. What do you think Nora and Torvald should have done differently?
  3. Gregers believed everyone must know the whole truth. Do you agree?
  4. What does it mean to think for yourself?
  5. Why do you think Ibsen ended A Doll's House with a door closing?

About ages 8 to 12. Read it together, or on your own.

Fyodor Dostoevsky (say dos-tuh-YEF-skee) was a Russian novelist. As a young man he was arrested for joining a group that discussed forbidden ideas, sentenced to death, and pardoned at the very last moment. He spent years in a prison camp in Siberia. Afterward he wrote some of the deepest novels ever written about right and wrong, faith and doubt.

The Brothers Karamazov is about three very different brothers. Dmitri is wild and passionate. Ivan is brilliant and full of questions. Alyosha, the youngest, is gentle and kind, and wants to help everyone. Their father is a selfish man who never took care of them, and the story is partly a mystery about what happened to him.

blocks.name: gb-karamazov-family
blocks.cap: The brothers and the people around them. Tap a name.

blocks.html: Alyosha's teacher, a wise old monk named Father Zosima, teaches that we are all responsible for each other and should love the whole world, "every grain of sand in it." At the end, Alyosha asks a group of schoolboys to always remember the good they felt when they were kind together.

For parents: this is a novel for older teens and adults. Its mystery is a murder, and some chapters discuss suffering, including Ivan's arguments, which the lesson summarizes without detail. Younger readers can enjoy the boys' chapters about Ilyusha (Book X) and the Epilogue.

🧩 Try this

Remember a kindness. Alyosha tells the boys that one good memory can help a person all their life. Write or draw a memory of a time someone was kind to you, or you to someone. Keep it somewhere you will see it.

📖 For teens and adults

The full lesson.

Fyodor Dostoevsky (1821–1881) was arrested in 1849 for taking part in a radical discussion circle, faced a firing squad, and was reprieved at the last moment; he served four years at hard labor in Siberia, reading only the New Testament. He returned a believing Orthodox Christian and the author of Crime and Punishment and other great novels. The Brothers Karamazov, his last, appeared as a magazine serial in 1879–80; he died a few months later. Constance Garnett's translation (1912) introduced it to many English readers.

blocks.name: gb-karamazov-family
blocks.cap: Our map of the Karamazovs and those around them.

blocks.html: Fyodor Karamazov, a greedy, mocking landowner, quarrels with his eldest son Dmitri over an inheritance and a woman, Grushenka. When Fyodor is found murdered, Dmitri is arrested. The middle brother Ivan, an intellectual, has been arguing that without God and immortality "everything is lawful" (in Garnett's words), and the servant Smerdyakov, rumored to be another son, has been listening. Alyosha, the youngest, a novice at the local monastery, tries to love them all.
In the book's most famous chapters, Ivan tells Alyosha why he cannot accept God's world: he cannot accept a world in which innocent children suffer, even if it all comes right in the end.

Then Ivan tells his prose poem "The Grand Inquisitor": Christ returns to 16th-century Spain, and an aged cardinal has him arrested. People cannot bear the freedom you gave them, the Inquisitor says; we have given them bread, miracles and authority instead. Christ says nothing and, at the end, kisses the old man. Alyosha, in turn, kisses Ivan.

Dostoevsky said the next book, the life and teachings of the elder Zosima, was his answer to Ivan, given not as an argument but as a way of living: humility, forgiveness, and the belief that each person is responsible to all.

Dmitri is convicted, though the reader learns more than the jury; Ivan breaks down under the weight of his own ideas; Dmitri finds in suffering a new sense of hope. The novel ends with Alyosha speaking to a group of schoolboys at the stone where their friend Ilyusha wanted to be buried:

Dostoevsky gave his strongest arguments to the doubter, Ivan, and many readers, believers and not, think Ivan's case is never answered in argument. Others find the answer in the lives of Zosima, Alyosha and the boys. The novel does not settle the question; it shows what each answer means in a human life.
Taking any one character as Dostoevsky's mouthpiece. He let each voice speak at full strength, so that the novel is, as later critics put it, a chorus of independent voices.

🔭 Going deeper

Context, the big questions, and how later books answered.

blocks.text: The Karamazovs in the great conversation

items: The Book of Job and Augustine asked why a good God allows suffering; Ivan presses the question harder than almost any other book.
Kierkegaard and Pascal, on this ladder, also spoke of faith as a choice of the whole person.
Nietzsche, Dostoevsky's contemporary, asked what happens to morality "beyond good and evil"; Ivan's "everything is lawful" is Dostoevsky's version of the question.
Freud, later on this ladder, wrote an essay on this novel.
Can a person be responsible for something they did not do, but wished or encouraged?
Is it possible to answer suffering with an argument, or only with love and action?
Why might people give up freedom for bread and certainty?
What does Alyosha mean when he says one good memory can save a person?

blocks.html:
💬 Talk about it together

  1. Which brother are you most like? Which would you want as a friend?
  2. Father Zosima taught that we are responsible for each other. What does that mean in a family?
  3. Why might someone find it hard to believe, even if they want to?
  4. Alyosha said a good memory from childhood can help someone all their life. Do you have one?
  5. Why do you think the novel ends with children, not with the trial?

Mark Twain (his real name was Samuel Clemens) grew up in a small town on the Mississippi River and later became a riverboat pilot. His most famous book is told by a boy named Huckleberry Finn, in Huck's own funny, rough way of talking.

Huck runs away from his cruel father. On an island he meets Jim, a man who has escaped from slavery because he was about to be sold away from his wife and children. The two float down the great river on a raft, mostly at night, having adventures with con men, feuding families and steamboats.

blocks.name: gb-huck-river
blocks.cap: Follow Huck and Jim down the Mississippi. Tap Next.

blocks.html: The story takes place before the Civil War, when slavery was legal in states like Missouri. Huck has been taught that helping Jim escape is wrong. But as he gets to know Jim, who is kind, wise and a true friend, Huck has to decide for himself what is right.

For parents: the novel uses the racial slurs common in its time and place, many times. This lesson never quotes them. Many families and teachers read it with older children together, talking about why the words appear and why they hurt; others start with a carefully edited edition or wait until the teen years.

🧩 Try this

Life on a raft. Huck says a raft feels "free and easy." Draw a raft big enough for two people to live on for weeks. What would you need: shelter, food, a lantern, a fishing line? Where would you sleep when it rained?

📖 For teens and adults

The full lesson.

Samuel Clemens (1835–1910) grew up in Hannibal, Missouri, a slave-holding river town, and piloted steamboats on the Mississippi before the Civil War. As "Mark Twain," a riverboat call meaning two fathoms of water, he became America's best-known humorist. He began Adventures of Huckleberry Finn in 1876, just after Tom Sawyer, and finished it years later. It was published in Britain in December 1884 and in the United States in February 1885. The story is set "forty to fifty years ago," in the 1830s or 1840s.

Twain wrote the whole book in Huck's voice, an uneducated boy's way of speaking, and in an opening note he explained that he used several regional dialects on purpose. Writers ever since have seen this as a turning point: serious American literature written in everyday American speech.

blocks.html: Huck fakes his own death to escape his violent father and meets Jim, who has fled Miss Watson because she planned to sell him down the river. They hope to reach Cairo, Illinois, and travel up the Ohio to the free states, but miss it in a fog. As they drift south, deeper into slave country, the raft becomes their home.
On shore Huck meets feuding families, a mob, and two swindlers, the "king" and the "duke," who take over the raft and finally sell Jim for a reward.
Huck has been taught by his whole society that helping Jim is a sin. He writes a letter to Miss Watson to tell her where Jim is, feels relieved, and then starts remembering:

The irony is the heart of the book. Huck thinks he is choosing wickedness; the reader sees he is choosing friendship and justice over the false morality of a slave-holding society. Twain later described the book as one where a sound heart and a deformed conscience come into collision, and conscience loses.

blocks.text: The language, and how readers have discussed it

blocks.html: The novel uses a racial slur for Black people more than two hundred times, as white people in that place and time commonly did. This lesson does not repeat it. Readers and schools have debated the book's language and its portrait of Jim for decades. Many see the novel as an attack on racism, showing Jim's humanity and the cruelty of slavery through a boy's eyes; others, including many Black readers and teachers, have argued that the slurs and some comic scenes wound students and reinforce stereotypes, and that the last chapters, where Tom Sawyer turns Jim's rescue into a game, undercut him. Some schools teach it with careful discussion, some offer other books, and some editions have replaced the word. The book was also banned in Concord, Massachusetts, in 1885, for coarseness, before these debates began.

Reading the novel as approving of the society it shows. Twain, who came to oppose slavery and racism, aimed his satire at the towns, churches and mobs on shore; but the debate about how the book should be read and taught is real, and worth having with care.

💬 Talk about it together

  1. What makes Jim a good friend to Huck?
  2. Huck had to choose between what people told him and what he felt was right. Have you ever had a choice like that?
  3. Why do you think some words are so hurtful? How should we talk about books that use them?
  4. Why do you think Huck and Jim felt free on the raft?
  5. If you could ask Jim one question, what would it be?
